entities.name: Gebhard (III) of Constance
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Gebhard (III) of Constance (d. 1110), Bishop of Constance from 1084 until his death, was a formidable prelate and a steadfast defender of papal authority against the Holy Roman Emperors during the height of the Investiture Controversy. His episcopacy was defined by unwavering opposition to Emperor Henry IV and later his son, Henry V, making him a central figure in the struggle between Sacerdotium and Imperium that profoundly reshaped medieval Europe. Operating from a strategically vital see in Swabia, he became a symbol of episcopal resistance to secular control over ecclesiastical appointments and a key ally for the reforming papacy.

Elevated to the bishopric by Pope Gregory VII in 1084, Gebhard immediately found himself at odds with Henry IV, who had appointed an anti-bishop, Otto of Ochsenstein. Gebhard's resolute refusal to acknowledge imperial jurisdiction or accept investiture from the emperor led to his repeated exiles, notably in 1085 and 1092, and the seizure of his episcopal properties. He was a prominent participant in several synods advocating for papal rights, including the Synod of Piacenza in 1095, where he openly supported Pope Urban II. His influence extended to securing the election of Berthold of Zähringen as Duke of Swabia, further weakening imperial power in the region. He also played a significant role in mediating the complex succession disputes within the empire, contributing to Henry V's initial rise against his father.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Gebhard (III) of Constance was a pivotal figure in the Investiture Controversy, whose unwavering defense of papal rights against two emperors significantly strengthened the Church's position and influenced the eventual resolution of the conflict, redefining Church-State relations in the Holy Roman Empire.
